beats.opener: Somewhere in there I got good at Excel. Not impressively — just genuinely useful. Enough that people started bringing me things.

And that's what got me to Amgen. They brought me in as a contractor for one project. Years of historical preclinical data — drug toxicology, pharmacology, real-time measurement — and they needed it out of spreadsheets and into a real database.

It is still the largest volume of data I have ever worked with.

beats.opener: And what made it hard wasn't the volume.
beats.rest:
No two of those spreadsheets were structured the same way. Same study type, same measurements, completely different layouts — because different people collected it, over years, and every one of them had their own way of doing it. There was no standard, so everybody invented one.

So the program couldn't just move data. It had to account for all of that variation. Read what somebody meant, not just what they typed, and land it in the same place every time.

That's the first time I understood what I actually liked. It wasn't the science.

It was that the data was in the wrong shape. And nobody had done anything wrong — a lot of reasonable people had each just done it slightly differently.

beats.cue: Say the tenure thing out loud

visual.title:

beats.opener: Topic one. Capitalize, or expense.
beats.rest:
Two calls I've made. Same four things for each one: what the rule wanted, what I did, how it came out, what I'd change.

One of them I made from the audit chair. The other one I'll get to.

Quick thing first, so it's not sitting there. I've never kept a fixed asset subledger. What I've done is make this call from the return, from the audit, and on my own work. The judgment I have. The posting is the part I'd learn.
beats.marks: Say the last paragraph evenly and then go straight into Example 1. No pause. You're sizing it, not apologizing.

visual.title:
It came in from
the repair guy.

beats.opener: First one's from a field audit. Details are disguised.
beats.rest:
People think a sales tax audit only looks at sales. It doesn't. We test what you bought too.

So I'm working the repairs and maintenance ledger. One vendor keeps showing up — small amounts, a few hundred at a time. Compressor service, filter changes, booth maintenance. All consistent with the account.

Then one entry from that same vendor is twenty thousand dollars.

Out-of-state. No tax charged. Equipment, freight, and installation on one invoice.

It's a spray booth. They bought the booth from the company that services their booths.
beats.marks: Slow on the last line. Let them get there a half-second before you say it.

visual.title:
Two rules.
One invoice.

a.lines:
Purchase price.
Installation labor is
excluded — Reg 1546.

b.lines:
Price plus freight
plus installation —
whatever it took to
get it working.

visual.tail: Same invoice, two different numbers. The rules are asking different questions.

beats.opener: And this is the part of the job I actually like. That one invoice gets measured twice, two different ways.
beats.rest:
For my purposes, the use tax measure starts with the purchase price. But installation labor is excluded under Regulation 1546.

For their books, under ASC 360, it's the opposite instruction. Freight and installation go into the asset's basis, because basis is whatever it took to get it in place and working.

Same invoice. Two different numbers. Not because anyone's wrong. Mine is asking what was purchased for use in California. Theirs is asking what the asset cost.
beats.marks: This is your credibility slide with Galvan. Unhurried, and don't apologize for the detail.

visual.title: Repair, or asset?

items.lead: The use tax was due either way
But it added capability, and it lasts years
Expensed to R&M, and never on the depreciation schedule

visual.callout: That same vendor's other invoices were genuine repairs. I left those alone.

beats.opener: Now, what did I actually decide? It's narrower than you'd think, and I want to be precise about it.
beats.rest:
The use tax didn't depend on the classification. Out-of-state tangible property, used in California, no tax paid to the vendor — use tax is due. Repair or asset, that doesn't move.

But the classification was wrong, and I raised it anyway, because it was their books. It added capability. They weren't fixing a booth, they were buying one. It lasts years. And it was expensed to repairs and never appeared on the depreciation schedule.

One more thing, and hold me to this. That same vendor's other invoices were real repairs. I left every one of them alone. If it only ever goes one way, it isn't judgment.
beats.marks: Say the repairs line plainly. The restraint is the point.

visual.kick: How it came out · what I'd change
visual.title: It held.
visual.sub: The vendor had a default account. The bill coded itself.

beats.opener: At the exit conference I walked the owner and their CPA through both pieces — what they owed, and separately, what their books had wrong. It held.
beats.rest:
And nobody was cheating. That vendor was set up with a default account in their books, and the default was repairs and maintenance — because for years, that's all that vendor had ever sent them. The bill came in, it coded itself, and nobody overrode it.

So there was a rule. It was just keyed on who sent the invoice instead of what was on it.

And that's why it sat for three years. Additions to the depreciation schedule get reviewed — by their CPA, by their lender, by me. Costs buried in repairs don't get reviewed by anyone. The coding didn't create the liability. It hid it.

So that's what I'd change. Not the audit. The rule that coded it. Hold onto that, I'll build it in Topic 2.
beats.marks: "Keyed on who sent the invoice instead of what was on it" is the setup for build 3. Land it.

visual.title:
He asked me about
an S-corp.
visual.sub: A construction client. Fixer-uppers. He'd just landed a contract bigger than anything he'd done.

beats.opener: Second one. Different chair. Nobody's books were on trial this time — somebody just asked me a question.
beats.rest:
Construction client of mine. Does fixer-uppers. He'd landed a contract bigger than anything he'd handled, and he wanted to know if he should elect S-corp.

The honest answer wasn't about the election. It was about what the election was going to cost him.

Once his receipts or his assets cross two hundred fifty thousand, he's filing a Schedule L and an M-1. That's a real balance sheet, and a reconciliation between his books and his return. Which means his books have to actually tie.

He was running a checkbook and a folder of receipts. That's a different business than the one he was asking about.
beats.marks: This is the slide that shows you advise on books. Don't rush it.

visual.kick: What the rule wanted · what I did
visual.title: Then he started buying equipment.

items.lead: Better, different, or brought back? Any one — capitalize
Or the safe harbor: $2,500 an invoice, no analysis
But only with a written policy, in place before the year starts

beats.opener: Then the equipment started coming. And now the call is mine, because I'm the one signing the return.
beats.rest:
Same test as the spray booth, different rulebook. Did it make the thing better, change what it does, or bring it back from broken? Any one of those and you capitalize it. None of them and it's a repair.

There's also a shortcut. The de minimis safe harbor lets you expense anything under twenty-five hundred an invoice and skip the analysis entirely.

But it has a condition. You need a written accounting policy, and it has to be in place before the tax year starts.

visual.kick: How it came out · what I'd change
visual.title:
Nobody had
written it down.
visual.sub: So we capitalized things we could have expensed. And he'd been my client the year before.

beats.opener: He didn't have one. So we couldn't use it.
beats.rest:
We capitalized a pile of small stuff that could have been deducted the day he bought it. Not because the rule said so. Because nobody had written one paragraph the previous December.

And I'll own my part of that. He'd been my client the year before. I never told him to write it.

So here's the lesson, and it's the same one as the spray booth. You don't get to decide at the end of the year and justify it backwards. The policy has to exist before the transaction does.

Classify on purpose, at the source, in writing. That's not my opinion. That's the regulation.
beats.marks: Land the last line and stop. It's the thesis of the whole talk, and the IRS is saying it, not you.

visual.title:
One had the wrong rule.
One had none.
visual.sub: Both got made at the point of entry, by whoever was closest.

beats.opener: Two calls. Neither one had the right rule behind it when it mattered.
beats.rest:
The first one had a rule. It was just keyed on the vendor instead of the invoice.

The second one had no rule at all, because nobody wrote it. Including me.

I picked those two on purpose. I could have shown you two wins.

I did the job by hand, and I know exactly where it hurts. So let me tell you what I'd build.
beats.marks: Through-line, pass 2. Straight into Topic 2, no pause.

visual.title:
The first
ninety days.
visual.sub: Learn the job honestly. Contribute like a builder.

beats.opener: Topic two. My first ninety days.
beats.rest: This is a learning plan and a contribution plan at the same time, and I want to be straight with you about which parts are which.

visual.title:
I haven't done
international accounting.
visual.sub: I understand the concepts in theory. I just don't have the reps — yet.

beats.opener: So let me say the obvious part out loud, because you already know it. I haven't done international accounting.
beats.rest:
What I do have is the standards. FAR tested consolidation and currency translation — ASC 830, intercompany eliminations, the CTA running through OCI instead of income. I understand the concepts in theory.

What I don't have is the reps.
beats.marks: PAUSE. Full stop. Do not rush to reassure them — the silence is the confidence.

beats.cue: But you've watched me do this
beats.opener: But you've just watched me do this four times.
beats.rest:
I hadn't done data architecture, and I wrote the VBA and moved it into a real database. I hadn't done Salesforce, and six months later I was the department. I hadn't done accounting at all, and I went and got a third bachelor's degree and passed four CPA exams.

I don't wait until I'm qualified. I go get qualified, and I do it while the work is happening.

So here's the ninety days.
beats.marks: This is the whole intro cashing in. Confident, not defensive. You're stating a record, not arguing.

visual.title: Four problems, and I know their names.

items.lead: Currency translation · ASC 830
items.sub: JPY and EUR into USD — and the CTA runs through OCI, not the income statement.

items.lead: Consolidation and eliminations
items.sub: Intercompany, investment, minority interest — in OneWorld or by hand.

items.lead: Transfer pricing
items.sub: Arm's-length documentation that survives Section 482 and a foreign authority's review.

items.lead: Indirect tax — VAT and Consumption Tax
items.sub: Which is the discipline I already run daily on California sales and use tax.

beats.opener: The terrain has four problems in it, and I already know their names.
beats.rest:
Currency translation under ASC 830 — Japan's yen and France's euro into dollars, with the translation adjustment running through OCI rather than income. Consolidation and eliminations — intercompany, investment, minority interest. Transfer pricing — documentation that has to survive both Section 482 and a foreign authority looking at the same transaction from the other side.

And indirect tax. VAT and Japanese Consumption Tax. Which is the one I'd argue I already do — that is the same discipline as California sales and use tax, and I run it every day.
beats.marks: Say the fourth one with a little more weight. It's the one place you're already an expert.

items.lead: Walk one full close manually
items.sub: Follow Japan's reporting package through translation and eliminations into the consolidated statements. Once, by hand.

items.lead: Sit with whoever does it now
items.sub: Not to review it. To learn it from the person who actually knows where it breaks.

items.lead: Map how OneWorld is configured
items.sub: Entities, currencies, elimination rules — what the system does versus what a human does after it.

beats.opener: Month one: do the job by hand.
beats.rest:
I want to follow one close all the way through manually. Take Japan's reporting package, walk it through translation and eliminations, and land it in the consolidated statements — once, by hand, slowly.

Not because that's efficient. Because that's the only way I've ever actually learned anything. And I want to sit with whoever does it today, not to review their work, but to find out where it breaks.

And I'll map how OneWorld is configured — what the system does automatically, versus what a person quietly fixes afterward.
beats.marks: You are deliberately echoing slide 7. Do not point at it — they'll feel it.

items.lead: Own real close tasks, under review
items.sub: Reconciliations and translation entries that are mine — checked by someone senior until they don't need to be.

items.lead: Time the close
items.sub: Where do the hours actually go? Nobody knows, because nobody has ever written it down.

items.lead: Pick one automation with the controller
items.sub: Highest pain, lowest risk. Their call, not mine.

beats.opener: Month two: feel where it hurts.
beats.rest:
By now I should be carrying real close tasks — reconciliations, translation entries — mine, under review by someone senior until that review stops being necessary.

And while I'm in there, I'm timing it. Where do the hours actually go? Most teams can't answer that, not because they're careless, but because nobody has ever had a reason to write it down.

Then I pick one automation with the controller. Highest pain, lowest risk. That's their call, not mine — I'm new.

visual.title: Build the thing that removes it.

items.lead: My slice of the close, fully owned
items.sub: No training wheels.

items.lead: The first automation live
items.sub: With a before-and-after number attached to it.

items.lead: Both documented well enough to survive me
items.sub: If it only works while I'm in the room, I haven't finished.

beats.opener: Month three: build the thing that removes it.
beats.rest:
My slice of the close is fully mine by then, no training wheels. The first automation is live, with a before-and-after number attached — not a claim, a measurement.

And both are documented well enough to survive me. If it only works while I'm in the room, I haven't actually finished it.

visual.title: You've seen this plan before.
visual.tail: It isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's the only way I've ever worked.

beats.opener: And I want to point at something, because I promised I would.
beats.rest:
This is the same plan I've run my entire career. I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

So: I do your close by hand, I find out exactly where it hurts, and then I build the thing that takes it away.

That isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's just the only way I've ever worked.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE pass 3 of 3 — the payoff of slide 7. Slow, and let the third row of the diagram sit before you speak over it.

visual.title:
Don't let it
code itself.
visual.sub: AI categorization is a control. Nobody tests it.

beats.opener: So here's the one idea I was asked to bring. It comes straight out of that spray booth.
beats.rest:
Ramp categorizes with AI. Most companies switch that on and treat it as a productivity feature.

But it isn't a feature. It's a control. Something is deciding what account a transaction lands in, thousands of times a month, and nothing is testing whether it was right.

If I walked into a business and asked what their detective control is over automated coding, most of them wouldn't have an answer.

So I'd build one.
beats.marks: "It's a control" is the sentence. Slow there. You are the person who audits the output of these systems — say it like someone who has seen it fail.

visual.title: Three signals. One invoice.

items.lead: The vendor default says repair
The amount says fifty times this vendor's median
The line items say equipment, freight, installation

visual.callout: Two of the three disagree with the default. That's the flag.

beats.opener: Here's how it would have caught my spray booth, the day it landed.
beats.rest:
Three independent signals look at the same invoice.

The vendor default says repair, because that's what that vendor always sends. The amount says this is about fifty times that vendor's own median. The line items say equipment, freight, and installation.

Two of the three disagree with the default.

And that's the rule. You don't flag on any single signal. You flag when they disagree — because the failure in my audit wasn't a bad rule. It was one rule, with nothing to check it against.
beats.marks: This is the loop closing on Topic 1. Let them make the connection before you spell it out.

visual.title: A rules layer in front of NetSuite.
visual.tail: The flag happens the moment the invoice lands — not three weeks later at close, and not three years later with me sitting across the table.

beats.opener: In practice it sits between Ramp and NetSuite, and it's boring, which is the point.
beats.rest:
The transaction lands. The AI assigns a category. Then three checks run against it — the vendor's usual account, the amount against that vendor's own history, and what the line items actually say.

If they agree, it posts. Nobody's day gets slower.

If they disagree, it routes to a short review queue where a person looks at it, once, while the invoice is still fresh and somebody still remembers what it was for.
beats.marks: Say "and not three years later with me sitting across the table" dry. Don't lean on it.

visual.title: And I'd rather say it than have you find it.

items.lead: A new vendor has no history
items.sub: So there's no median to compare against. The first few invoices from anyone always route to review.

items.lead: Too few invoices to have a baseline
items.sub: Below about five, the statistic is noise. Fall back to a flat threshold instead of pretending.

items.lead: Flagging everything is worse than flagging nothing
items.sub: A queue nobody works is a control that only looks like one. Tie the threshold to performance materiality — flag what could matter, not what's merely unusual.

items.lead: It has to cut both ways
items.sub: It should catch things wrongly capitalized too. Same discipline as the repairs I left alone.

beats.opener: And here's what would make it fail, because I'd rather say it than have you find it.
beats.rest:
A new vendor has no history, so there's nothing to compare against — those always go to review until there's a baseline. Below about five invoices the statistic is just noise, so it falls back to a flat threshold rather than pretending to know something.

One technical note. It compares against the median, not the average, because an average gets wrecked by exactly the outlier you're hunting for. One big purchase last year and the average stops flagging anything.

And the real risk isn't statistical, it's human. If it flags two hundred things a month, everybody ignores it, and now you have something worse than no control — because people believe something is watching. So the threshold ties to materiality.

Last one: it has to catch things wrongly capitalized too, not just wrongly expensed. Same discipline as the repairs I left alone.
beats.marks: This is the credibility slide. Naming the failure modes yourself is worth more than the idea. Unhurried.

visual.title: Remove one manual step a month.

items.lead: Measure the close first
items.sub: Where do the hours actually go? Nobody can answer that, because nobody has had a reason to write it down.

items.lead: Then a package pre-check
items.sub: Automated completeness and tie-out on subsidiary packages, before a human opens them.

items.lead: Every build ships with a before-and-after number
items.sub: Measured, not claimed.

beats.opener: And that's the first one, not the only one. The method underneath is the same every month.
beats.rest:
Measure where the hours actually go, then remove exactly one manual step. Small builds, each shipped with a before-and-after number.

Most closes never get faster. Not because anyone's bad at their job — because everybody owns their piece, their piece works, and nobody owns "faster."

I'm offering to own faster.
beats.marks: PAUSE before "I'm offering to own faster." That's the line you want them repeating afterwards.

visual.title:
And when the auditors
get bigger.
visual.sub: I'd go get the Certified Internal Auditor — so I'm already that person before the audit shows up, not during it.

beats.opener: One thing beyond ninety days, because Vast is going to keep scaling and the audit gets bigger with it.
beats.rest:
At some point the external audit stops being a formality. Somebody on the inside has to already speak that language — to know what they're going to ask for before they ask, and to have it ready.

I'd go get the Certified Internal Auditor for that. Not because the role requires it. Because I'd rather be that person before the audit shows up than during it.

And I want to be honest about the timeline — that's three parts and about a year. It is not a ninety-day promise.
beats.marks: The honesty about the timeline is doing real work here. Do not skip it to sound more impressive.

items.lead: My close tasks owned
items.sub: Not shadowed. Owned.

items.lead: One automation live, with numbers
items.sub: Measured, not claimed.

items.lead: And a close that gets a step faster every month after that
items.sub: Because somebody finally owns faster.

beats.opener: So, in ninety days: my close tasks owned — not shadowed, owned.
beats.rest:
One automation live, with a real number attached to it.

And a close that gets a step faster every month after that, because somebody finally owns faster.

visual.title:
I was the guy
entering the data.
visual.sub: Then I built the system. I'd like to do that here.

beats.opener: I started by telling you I was the guy entering the data.
